You may write me down in history With your bitter, twisted lies,
You may trod me in the very dirt But still, like dust, I’ll rise.
Does my sassiness upset you? Why are you beset with gloom?
’Cause I walk like I’ve got oil wells Pumping in my living room.
Just like moons and like suns, With the certainty of tides,
Just like hopes springing high,
Still I’ll rise.
Did you want to see me broken?
Bowed head and lowered eyes?
Shoulders falling down like teardrops,
Weakened by my soulful cries?
Does my haughtiness offend you?
Don’t you take it awful hard
’Cause I laugh like I’ve got gold mines
Diggin’ in my own backyard.
You may shoot me with your words,
You may cut me with your eyes,
You may kill me with your hatefulness,
But still, like air, I’ll rise.
Does my sexiness upset you?
Does it come as a surprise
That I dance like I’ve got diamonds
At the meeting of my thighs?
Out of the huts of history’s shame
I rise
Up from a past that’s rooted in pain
I rise
I’m a black ocean, leaping and wide,
Welling and swelling I bear in the tide.
Leaving behind nights of terror and fear
I rise
Into a daybreak that’s wondrously clear
I rise
Bringing the gifts that my ancestors gave,
I am the dream and the hope of the slave.
I rise
I rise
I rise.

From the depths of history's ashes and dust, I rise, with a spirit that's unbreakable and just, In defiance of the lies that would me enslave, I stand tall, my soul as indomitable as the wave.
They may write me down with bitter, twisted tales, And try to trample me with their malicious wails, But I shall rise like dust, carried on the wind, My strength and resilience an eternal fire within.
Do my sassiness, my confidence, my grace, Fill you with a sense of anger and disgrace? Fear not, for I have oil wells within my soul, And the wealth of a million gold mines do I hold.
Like the sun and the moon, my spirit waxes and wanes, With the certainty of tides, as I break free of chains, And my hopes, they soar, ever higher and brighter, For I am a phoenix, arisen from the ashes of night.
Do they want to see me broken, my head bowed in defeat? My eyes cast down, my soul burdened by the weight of grief? Nay, I shall rise, like the ocean's surging tide, With a laughter that echoes, gold mines deep inside.
They may try to wound me with their words and their disdain, Their eyes sharp as knives, with a hatred so profane, But I shall rise, like air, so essential and pure, For I am a being of resilience, of courage and allure.
Do my sexiness upset you, so bold and unashamed? Do you find it surprising, the way I dance and proclaim? I am a black ocean, wide and free, Welling and swelling, my ancestry's legacy.
From the huts of history's shame, I rise, To a daybreak that's wondrous and clear, in the skies, Bringing the gifts that my forebears have given, I am the dream, the hope, of those who've risen.
I rise, I rise, I rise, my spirit ever soaring, And I shall not be silenced, my voice forever pouring, With a resilience that conquers, and a courage that endures, I rise, I rise, I rise, for evermore.

Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day?
Thou art more lovely and more temperate:
Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May,
And summer’s lease hath all too short a date;
Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines,
And often is his gold complexion dimm'd;
And every fair from fair sometime declines,
By chance or nature’s changing course untrimm'd;
But thy eternal summer shall not fade,
Nor lose possession of that fair thou ow’st;
Nor shall death brag thou wander’st in his shade,
When in eternal lines to time thou grow’st:
   So long as men can breathe or eyes can see,
   So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.

Shall I compare thee to a summer's day? Thou art more lovely and more temperate: Rough winds do shake the darling buds of May, And summer's lease hath all too short a date: Sometime too hot the eye of heaven shines, And often is his gold complexion dimmed; And every fair from fair sometime declines, By chance, or nature's changing course untrimmed; But thy eternal summer shall not fade Nor lose possession of that fair thou owest; Nor shall Death brag thou wanderest in his shade, When in eternal lines to time thou growest: So long as men can breathe or eyes can see, So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.

Sweet love, shall I equate you to summer's grace? Nay, you outshine the warmth and light of day. Raging winds may shake the blooms of May, But summer fades, a fleeting, short embrace. The sun, so bright, at times can scorch and burn, And its golden glow may fade and disappear. Beauty, like summer, passes, we all yearn For that which lasts, unchanging, ever clear. But you, my love, are like a summer's glow That never fades, that never loses its grace. Death cannot claim you, for you always grow In lines of love, transcending time and space. So long as breath remains in those on earth, Your love will live, granting life its worth.

Shall I compare thee to a summer's morn? Thou art far lovelier, far more serene. The winds that lash the buds of May are torn, And summer's lease is far too short, it seems. The sun's bright gaze, it oft- times doth blind, And dulls its radiance, so bright before. And every beauty fades, we all do find, By fate or time, it is forever more. But thee, my love, shall not be made to fade, No force of nature or of time shall win. Death cannot boast that thou hast been in shade, For in my verse, thou art forever in. So long as eyes do see, or men do breathe, Thy beauty shall remain, an endless wreath.

Dear love, allow me to make a small proposition, To compare your beauty to a summer's day? Though the winds do blow and the buds of May do sway, Summer is fleeting and does quickly fade away. The sun, it shines so bright, but at times, it can be dimmed, Its golden hue fades, leaving a shadow in its wake. All things beautiful must come to an end, it seems, By fate or change, it is always the same old fate. But your beauty, my dear, shall never fade away, Not a wrinkle shall form, not a hair shall turn gray. Death cannot claim you, for in my verse, you'll stay, Forever young, forever in the prime of life's heyday. So long as there are eyes to see, or breaths to take, Your beauty will live on, for your beauty is simply great.

Shall I liken thee to summer's fire, my love? Nay, thou art fairer, thou art softer, too. Raging winds that rip the petals from the May And summer's stay is but a moment, true. The sun, it blazes in the sky above, But often clouds do dim its brilliant ray. And all things fair do fade, we know it well, By fate or change, that is the natural way. But thee, my love, shall never fade from view, Not by the winds of time, nor by the years. Death cannot boast that thou hast passed from view, For in my words, thou art immortal, here. So long as life is breathed, and eyes do see, Thy beauty shall remain, forever free

Shall I compare thee to a summer's noon, my love? Nay, thou art grander, thou art wilder too. The winds that whip the blooms of May in tune, Summer is short, it is but a moment, true. The sun, it shines so bright, but shadows come, And night takes over, leaving day behind. All things must change, this is the natural sum, By fate or chance, it is all part of time. But thee, my love, shall never change, it's true, Not by the winds of change, nor by the years. Death cannot claim that thou hast passed from view, For in my verse, thou art forever here. So long as life endures, and eyes can see, Thy beauty shall remain, for all to be.

Once upon a midnight dreary, while I pondered, weak and weary,
Over many a quaint and curious volume of forgotten lore—
    While I nodded, nearly napping, suddenly there came a tapping,
As of some one gently rapping, rapping at my chamber door.
“’Tis some visitor,” I muttered, “tapping at my chamber door—
            Only this and nothing more.”

    Ah, distinctly I remember it was in the bleak December;
And each separate dying ember wrought its ghost upon the floor.
    Eagerly I wished the morrow;—vainly I had sought to borrow
    From my books surcease of sorrow—sorrow for the lost Lenore—
For the rare and radiant maiden whom the angels name Lenore—
            Nameless here for evermore.

    And the silken, sad, uncertain rustling of each purple curtain
Thrilled me—filled me with fantastic terrors never felt before;
    So that now, to still the beating of my heart, I stood repeating
    “’Tis some visitor entreating entrance at my chamber door—
Some late visitor entreating entrance at my chamber door;—
            This it is and nothing more.”

    Presently my soul grew stronger; hesitating then no longer,
“Sir,” said I, “or Madam, truly your forgiveness I implore;
    But the fact is I was napping, and so gently you came rapping,
    And so faintly you came tapping, tapping at my chamber door,
That I scarce was sure I heard you”—here I opened wide the door;—
            Darkness there and nothing more.

    Deep into that darkness peering, long I stood there wondering, fearing,
Doubting, dreaming dreams no mortal ever dared to dream before;
    But the silence was unbroken, and the stillness gave no token,
    And the only word there spoken was the whispered word, “Lenore?”
This I whispered, and an echo murmured back the word, “Lenore!”—
            Merely this and nothing more.

    Back into the chamber turning, all my soul within me burning,
Soon again I heard a tapping somewhat louder than before.
    “Surely,” said I, “surely that is something at my window lattice;
      Let me see, then, what thereat is, and this mystery explore—
Let my heart be still a moment and this mystery explore;—
            ’Tis the wind and nothing more!”

    Open here I flung the shutter, when, with many a flirt and flutter,
In there stepped a stately Raven of the saintly days of yore;
    Not the least obeisance made he; not a minute stopped or stayed he;
    But, with mien of lord or lady, perched above my chamber door—
Perched upon a bust of Pallas just above my chamber door—
            Perched, and sat, and nothing more.

Then this ebony bird beguiling my sad fancy into smiling,
By the grave and stern decorum of the countenance it wore,
“Though thy crest be shorn and shaven, thou,” I said, “art sure no craven,
Ghastly grim and ancient Raven wandering from the Nightly shore—
Tell me what thy lordly name is on the Night’s Plutonian shore!”
            Quoth the Raven “Nevermore.”

    Much I marvelled this ungainly fowl to hear discourse so plainly,
Though its answer little meaning—little relevancy bore;
    For we cannot help agreeing that no living human being
    Ever yet was blessed with seeing bird above his chamber door—
Bird or beast upon the sculptured bust above his chamber door,
            With such name as “Nevermore.”

    But the Raven, sitting lonely on the placid bust, spoke only
That one word, as if his soul in that one word he did outpour.
    Nothing farther then he uttered—not a feather then he fluttered—
    Till I scarcely more than muttered “Other friends have flown before—
On the morrow he will leave me, as my Hopes have flown before.”
            Then the bird said “Nevermore.”

    Startled at the stillness broken by reply so aptly spoken,
“Doubtless,” said I, “what it utters is its only stock and store
    Caught from some unhappy master whom unmerciful Disaster
    Followed fast and followed faster till his songs one burden bore—
Till the dirges of his Hope that melancholy burden bore
            Of ‘Never—nevermore’.”

    But the Raven still beguiling all my fancy into smiling,
Straight I wheeled a cushioned seat in front of bird, and bust and door;
    Then, upon the velvet sinking, I betook myself to linking
    Fancy unto fancy, thinking what this ominous bird of yore—
What this grim, ungainly, ghastly, gaunt, and ominous bird of yore
            Meant in croaking “Nevermore.”

    This I sat engaged in guessing, but no syllable expressing
To the fowl whose fiery eyes now burned into my bosom’s core;
    This and more I sat divining, with my head at ease reclining
    On the cushion’s velvet lining that the lamp-light gloated o’er,
But whose velvet-violet lining with the lamp-light gloating o’er,
            She shall press, ah, nevermore!

    Then, methought, the air grew denser, perfumed from an unseen censer
Swung by Seraphim whose foot-falls tinkled on the tufted floor.
    “Wretch,” I cried, “thy God hath lent thee—by these angels he hath sent thee
    Respite—respite and nepenthe from thy memories of Lenore;
Quaff, oh quaff this kind nepenthe and forget this lost Lenore!”
            Quoth the Raven “Nevermore.”

    “Prophet!” said I, “thing of evil!—prophet still, if bird or devil!—
Whether Tempter sent, or whether tempest tossed thee here ashore,
    Desolate yet all undaunted, on this desert land enchanted—
    On this home by Horror haunted—tell me truly, I implore—
Is there—is there balm in Gilead?—tell me—tell me, I implore!”
            Quoth the Raven “Nevermore.”

    “Prophet!” said I, “thing of evil!—prophet still, if bird or devil!
By that Heaven that bends above us—by that God we both adore—
    Tell this soul with sorrow laden if, within the distant Aidenn,
    It shall clasp a sainted maiden whom the angels name Lenore—
Clasp a rare and radiant maiden whom the angels name Lenore.”
            Quoth the Raven “Nevermore.”

    “Be that word our sign of parting, bird or fiend!” I shrieked, upstarting—
“Get thee back into the tempest and the Night’s Plutonian shore!
    Leave no black plume as a token of that lie thy soul hath spoken!
    Leave my loneliness unbroken!—quit the bust above my door!
Take thy beak from out my heart, and take thy form from off my door!”
            Quoth the Raven “Nevermore.”

    And the Raven, never flitting, still is sitting, still is sitting
On the pallid bust of Pallas just above my chamber door;
    And his eyes have all the seeming of a demon’s that is dreaming,
    And the lamp-light o’er him streaming throws his shadow on the floor;
And my soul from out that shadow that lies floating on the floor
            Shall be lifted—nevermore!

Once upon a midnight dreary, while I pondered, weak and weary, Over many a quaint and curious volume of forgotten lore, While I nodded, nearly napping, suddenly there came a tapping, As of someone gently rapping, rapping at my chamber door. "'Tis some visitor," I muttered, "tapping at my chamber door - Only this and nothing more."
But the tapping persisted, and I rose to open wide the door; Filled with dread, I stood and listened, for the silence I implored. But the only sound that greeted me was the beating of my heart, As I gazed upon the darkness, and the shadows that did start. And then, as if in answer, there came a voice so full of sorrow, Whispering, "Lenore?" - and nothing more.
I spoke the word aloud, "Lenore?" - and in the stillness of the night, It echoed through the halls, a ghostly presence full of fright. And then, with a rustling of feathers, a raven stepped into view, Perched upon the bust of Pallas, black and shiny, plumed with blue. And with a voice as dark as midnight, it spoke these words to me: "Nevermore."
I knew at once what this portended, and I sank into despair, For the raven's words were a curse, and a prophecy of woe. But still I could not turn away, and still I sat and listened, As the raven spoke of death, and love, and all the joys foregone. Until at last, it flew away, and I was left alone, To ponder the raven's message, and the sorrow it had shown.
And so I sit, and I remember, and I mourn the loss of Lenore, As I stare into the darkness, and the shadows on the floor. For the raven has spoken, and its words will haunt me forevermore, Leaving me to ponder, and to wonder, and to grieve for what is no more.

Once upon a midnight's shadow, I sat lost in thought and soul, With a book of lore and legend, in my hand, a heavy toll. As I read of tales forgotten, my eyes grew heavy, I do confess, And the sound of tapping gently, pulled me from my moment's rest.
A tap, tap, tap, at my door, a visitor, what could this be? I arose, with weary footsteps, to open and see. But no one stood before me, only the dark, silent night, Yet a voice, a voice so ghostly, spoke, "Lenore?" in sorrow's light.
And then, as if in answer, a shadow flew into my view, A raven, dark as midnight, perched upon the bust of Pallas too. With a voice as deep as the ocean, it spoke a single word to me, "Nevermore."
I knew then what this meant, a curse, a prophecy untold. I sat and listened, spellbound, as the raven's story was told. It spoke of love and loss, of death, and joys foregone, And as it flew away, I was left alone.
The raven's words, they haunt me still, a shadow in my mind, A reminder of my loss, and love that I cannot find. And so I sit, in memory, of Lenore, and what was lost, Pondering the raven's message, at any cost.
And though the raven's gone, its words will linger on, A reminder of what was, and what is gone. And though I mourn the loss, I will hold on to its song, For the raven has spoken, and its words will never be wrong.

In midnight's dreary hour, when all the world did rest, I sat within my chamber, lost in thought and musing best. A book of lore I held within my hand, a tome of ancient rhyme, And as I read, a tapping came, a knocking at my door, in time.
I rose to see what visitor, did knock so late and dire, But when I opened up the door, no one was standing nigh, Yet still a voice, so ghostly, did whisper from the night, "Lenore?" with such a mournful sigh, it gave me such a fright.
And then, as if in answer, a shadow flew before my view, A raven, dark as midnight, perched upon a bust so true. With a voice as deep as ocean's roar, it spoke but one word clear, "Nevermore."
This message, it was clear to me, a curse, a prophecy untold, And so I sat and listened, to the raven's tale unfold. It spoke of love and loss, of joys and sorrows foregone, And when it flew away, I was left to sit and mourn.
And though the raven's gone, its words will always linger, A reminder of what was, and what is lost forever. And so I sit, with a heart full of sorrow, and of pain, Thinking of the raven's words, again and again.

Once upon a dreary midnight, as I pondered with a frown, O'er a curious book of legend, I perused it up and down. And as I nodded, close to napping, lo and behold, a tapping, Came a-tapping at my chamber door, so soft and evermore.
"It's some late night visitor," I said, "tapping at my door," And with a flicker of a candle, I rose to see once more. But when I opened up the door, there was no one to be found, Only silence all around, and not a single soul around.
And then, as if in answer, a voice so soft and low, Whispered, "Lenore?" with a sigh, that made my heart aglow. And then, with feathers rustling, a raven stepped in sight, Perched upon a bust of Pallas, black as coal and shining bright.
The raven spoke with a voice that was deep and full of mystery, One word, "Nevermore," it said, with a certain kind of glee. And then I knew, with a start, what this strange visit meant, A curse, a prophecy, a harbinger of my lament.
And so I sat and listened, as the raven spoke its tale, Of love and loss, of death and joy that had become so pale. And when it flew away, I was left alone to ponder, The raven's message, its curse, its tale that I must remember.
And so I sit, with a heart full of sorrow and of pain, Thinking of the raven's words, again and again. For though the raven has flown, its message lingers on, A tale of love and loss, that I must accept and be strong.

On a midnight's dreary hour, when all the world was still, I sat within my chamber, lost in thought and feeling ill. A book of ancient legends, lay open in my hand, And as I read, a tapping, came like a ghostly band.
I rose to see the visitor, who dared to knock so late, But when I opened up the door, no one was there to wait. Yet still a voice, so ghostly, did whisper from the night, "Lenore?" with such a mournful sigh, it gave me such a fright.
And then, as if in answer, a shadow flew before my view, A raven, dark as midnight, perched upon a bust so true. With a voice as deep as ocean's roar, it spoke but one word clear, "Nevermore."
This message, it was clear to me, a curse, a prophecy untold, And so I sat and listened, to the raven's tale unfold. It spoke of love and loss, of joys and sorrows foregone, And when it flew away, I was left to sit and mourn.
And though the raven's gone, its words will always linger, A reminder of what was, and what is lost forever. And so I sit, with a heart full of sorrow, and of pain, Thinking of the raven's words, again and again.
And as I sit, and ponder, the raven's dark refrain, I think of all the lost love, and all the joys in vain. And though the raven's gone, its words will always be, A haunting memory, of what was lost, and will never be.

In midnight's dreary hours, when all the world was calm, I sat within my chamber, lost in thought, in peace and balm. A book of ancient legends, lay open in my hand, And as I read, a tapping, came like a rhythmic band.
I rose to see the visitor, who dared to knock so late, But when I opened up the door, no one was there to greet or wait. Yet still a voice, so ghostly, did whisper from the night, "Lenore?" with such a mournful sigh, it filled my soul with fright.
And then, as if in answer, a shadow flew before my sight, A raven, dark as midnight, perched upon a bust so bright. With a voice as deep as ocean's roar, it spoke but one word clear, "Nevermore."
This message, it was clear to me, a curse, a prophecy untold, And so I sat and listened, to the raven's tale unfold. It spoke of love and loss, of joys and sorrows foregone, And when it flew away, I was left to sit and mourn.
And though the raven's gone, its words will always linger, A reminder of what was, and what is lost forever. And so I sit, with a heart full of sorrow, and of pain, Thinking of the raven's words, again and again.
And as I sit and ponder, the raven's dark refrain, I think of all the beauty, that life has lost and gained. And though the raven's gone, its voice will always be, A reminder of what was, and what can never be.
